item.title: Aristotle and the Sephirot
item.description:
Aristotle

Understanding Aristotle is the solution to many problems which make cognition cloudy and misconstrued today. All manner of total architechonic is present in his Organon, whether it be the sciences, spirituality, or a practical way to ground our thinking in the basic structures of reality itself. When we find ourselves lost in the sea of subjective opining and ungrounded assertions or skepticism, Aristotle’s work stands as a vestige from a time when the love of wisdom was prioritized, providing us an antidote of clarity and contemplation. Yet despite this utility, Aristotle is rarely given his due. In many modern curricula, he’s reduced to a footnote in the history of logic, remembered only for a dry linguistic formalism. In other circles, he is misinterpreted as a systematizer of mere subjective categories, a pioneer of taxonomy in thought, whose primary achievement was to create a filing system for our own mental projections. These miss the very real organic core of his body of work. Aristotle’s work in logic is describing the real insofar as they are the highest beings that are in the world, and so his primary aim was in answering the question of what is. It then makes sense that Aristotle’s Categories begin first and foremost with substance, because for him, the world is not a collection of events or floating properties, it is at the highest level a world of things, of self-subsisting entities. Substance is named as the primary reality, the being that underlies all others. And so a horse is a being, as is a man, and as is a tree. Their qualities, quantities, and relations are all predicated of the substance and cannot exist on their own. Beginning with substance, Aristotle establishes an objective anchor for thought by allowing it to discern the structure of what is.

This structure is organic. As opposed to a mechanical view, which would see the world as a clockwork of interacting parts, where the whole is simply the sum of its pieces and change is an indifferent function of that interaction, Aristotle’s view posits a unity where the parts have meaning and function only in relation to the whole. This is what it means to act organically; to be organic is to be a self-subsisting whole that contains within itself an internal principle of movement and development, or a telos. Logos speaks to the intelligibility of this structure as the structure itself that makes a thing what it is, and what makes it knowable. Importantly, this implies a pervadingness of intelligibility or logic in both the subject and the world. In other words, what it says about both the organic system and the subject that there is a commensurability to them with respect to intelligibility and logos? It says that both we are intelligent, and that there is intelligence in the world, that we have the capability to be logical, and so does the world. Likewise, logic is not a tool we impose on the world, but rather the very language of the world as it self-articulates. Aristotle’s syllogism, for instance, is the formal expression of how the universal (the species, the form) is mediated through the particular to produce new, knowledge. It can be said that the deduction of syllogism is not in our minds, it is in the divine mind of spirit’s self communion. To think logically is to think in harmony with the logos of reality itself. While some may see the classic syllogism: “All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore, Socrates is mortal” as a tool for argumentation, it is in reality the logical structure by which mediated knowledge is self-articulated by the whole. This is precisely why thinkers like G.W.F. Hegel would make the syllogism the absolute form of all reality. In many ways, Hegel belongs in the tradition of Aristotle, providing defense against the claim of the categories being mere enumeration, and proving the absolute character of logic. The aim of this article is not to prove any of these things, however it is worth exploring for those not convinced of teleology, logic, and so forth and so on.

Sephirot

Ultimately, Aristotle’s Categories represent the West’s attempt to articulate an ultimate reality. The correlative Eastern attempt (roughly) is found via the Kabbalistic Sephirot of the Jewish people. Etz Chaim, or the Tree of Life, is the name for this structure. It advances a system of ten divine emanations. Unlike a modern, who sees the human as a chance conglomeration of chemicals, ancient Jewish sages saw the human form as a kind of enacted scripture, a testament to the creative forces of the universe. They perceived that from the farthest reaches of the cosmos, ten distinct spiritual forces converge upon the human being, shaping him from without, and animating from within. These forces are creative powers, they are the very structure of reality made manifest. The “Tree” is thus a map of this interfacing between divinity and humanity, showing how practically the upper celestial worlds pour their influences down into the earthly realm, culminating in the creation and sustenance of mankind.

The observant among you may have noticed a similarity already. Why ten in both Aristotle and Sephirot? The number carries both an esoteric and anthropological significance. Firstly, and of course most intuitively, it is the number of our own fingers. For the ancient peoples, the body was the first and most immediate instrument of the understanding. As Manly P Hall states in The Secret Teachings of All Ages,:

THE oldest, the most profound, the most universal of all symbols is the human body. The Greeks, Persians, Egyptians, and Hindus considered a philosophical analysis of man’s triune nature to be an indispensable part of ethical and religious training. The Mysteries of every nation taught that the laws, elements, and powers of the universe were epitomized in the human constitution; that everything which existed outside of man had its analogue within man. The universe, being immeasurable in its immensity and inconceivable in its profundity, was beyond mortal estimation. Even the gods themselves could comprehend but a part of the inaccessible glory which was their source. When temporarily permeated with divine enthusiasm, man may transcend for a brief moment the limitations of his own personality and behold in part that celestial effulgence in which all creation is bathed. But even in his periods of greatest illumination man is incapable of imprinting upon the substance of his rational soul a perfect image of the multiform expression of celestial activity. Recognizing the futility of attempting to cope intellectually with that which transcends the comprehension of the rational faculties, the early philosophers turned their attention from the inconceivable Divinity to man himself, with in the narrow confines of whose nature they found manifested all the mysteries of the external spheres. As the natural outgrowth of this practice there was fabricated a secret theological system in which God was considered as the Grand Man and, conversely, man as the little god. Continuing this analogy, the universe was regarded as a man and, conversely, man as a miniature universe. The greater universe was termed the Macrocosm–the Great World or Body– and the Divine Life or spiritual entity controlling its functions was called the Macroprosophus. Man’s body, or the individual human universe, was termed the Microcosm, and the Divine Life or spiritual entity controlling its functions was called the Microprosophus.

The human hand, with its ten digits, was a symbol of completeness and action, the means by which the human being grasps and interacts with the world. It is no coincidence that our base 10 number system arises, given this biological fact (I, for one, still prefer base-60). To the ancient mind, the cosmos in its full breadth was mirrored in the completeness of the human form, with ten representing the totality of a cycle or a system. The significance was not lost on the Greek esoteric tradition, which deeply influence Western philosophical and spiritual currents. The Pythagoreans, as invoked by Aristotle himself, conceived of a table of 10 opposites, ten couples of opposite categories: Limited and Unlimited, Odd and Even, Unity and Plurality, Right and Left, Male and Female, At Rest and In Motion, Straight and Curved, Light and Darkness, Good and Evil, and Square and Oblong. Aristotle noted that Alcmaeon of Croton also viewed pairs of opposites as fundamental principles, although he was unsure whether Alcmaeon influenced the Pythagoreans or vice versa. Associating the left-hand column (the former of the pairs) with “good” qualities, the table may have been known in his time, possibly at Plato’s Academy, although Aristotle mainly used it to support his arguments. The reason they are enumerated as ten is because Iamblichus and the Pythagoreans held the number ten (the Decad) in the highest esteem. For Pythagoras, the Tetraktys was the very symbol of cosmic order, encompassing the sum of all possibilities. It was considered the holiest of numbers, representing the universe itself as a perfect all-encompassing whole. The number four signified the elements, the directions, the seasons, and their sum (1+ 2 + 3 + 4 = 10) ten signified the completed world. This Greek reverence for the decad surely resonates with the Kabbalistic structure, where the ten Sephirot are the complete emanation of the divine, and it goes without saying that the influence Pythagoras had on Aristotle is not to be discounted. Jewish numerology and mysticism similarly has 10 standing as a number representing the finality of union between the natural and supranatural: Ten Commandments, ten plagues, ten divine utterances, ten generations between Adam and Noah and Noah and Abraham, and Yud as the tenth letter in the Hebrew alphabet that links unity (Yehudi) with God (YHWH) and the particularized Jewish people (Yehudi), to name a few significances.

Now, the system of Sephirot is most distinctly represented in the form of Adam Kadmon, also known as the “Primordial Man”. For clarity, this is an archetype rather than a physical being, a kind of schematic of the spiritual structure of the universe as reflected in humanity. The ten Sephirot are distributed as the “body parts” of this perfect cosmic human, creating a symbolic mapping which shows the spiritual forces as actual and graduated forces in an organic hierarchy, moving from the most spiritual to the most earthly. Kether, or the crown, is the first Sephirah, the first emanation from the divine, an unfathomable “nothing” that contains all potentiality. It is the site of origin from which all remaining Sephirot unfold, corresponding to the “crown” of the cosmic human, the highest spiritual center. Chokmah (Wisdom) and Binah (Intelligence) are the eyes of Adam Kadmon. Chokmah is comparable to the intuitive flash of insight, versus Binah as the discerning principle of comprehension and organization. These two forces structure our perception of the cosmos. Chesed (Freedom) and Geburah (Severity/Strength) correspond to the right and left hands. The right hand (Chesed) is expansive, loving, and represents freedom and kindness, while the left (Geburah) is restrictive, powerful, and represents judgement and overcoming. These shape our action and experience. Tipereth (Beauty) is the central Sephirah, it is the torso, or heart of Adam Kadmon, the balance point of the higher and lower forces. That is to say, it is the principle of harmony and beauty that is the true center of the human being, despite what one may encounter. Netsah (Endurance) and Hod (Majesty) are the legs or thighs. Netsah is the force of movement and endurance, that inevitable overcoming might. Hod is the inner feeling, specifically the splendor of inner life. These represent the overcoming of the world in order to venture forth, and the reconnection and compassion to and with the world respectively. Next, there is Yesod (Foundation). This is the place of circumcision, the foundational and generative power. It is the force that grounds us, the sexual and creative impulse that is the physical foundation for manifesting life. Finally, there is Malkuth (Kingdom). This is the feet, the final and lowest Sephirah. It is the complete manifestation of all preceding forces in the physical world, the “field” or “kingdom” of our earthly activity.

To merely enumerate these names is akin to possessing the alphabet without the ability to read. This is precisely the point made by thinkers like Raymond of Sabunde, The Sephirot become dry and appalling abstractions when divorced from their experiential verity. The real significance lies in how these forces are to be experienced and not in the mere remembering of the concepts. The student must practice this devotion so assiduously that the Idea begins to come alive within them, and then it can truly be said that one comprehends the Sephirot. Aristotle is often left to the wayside partly for this reason, the formalistic aspect of logic is grasped as representing the whole of the significance of the categories, and so the Idea which Aristotle envisioned does not come alive in the soul of the individual. Ancient Jewish sages certainly did not intend for their teachings as information to be downloaded and manipulated as Aristotle is now. The Sephirot for them were spiritual letters. Just as the physical alphabet is useless if one cannot combine the letters to form words and sentences that convey meaning, the Sephirot are useless if one cannot spontaneously jumble them together in their own mind to read the spiritual world. The goal was to learn a living alphabet where the letters corresponded to the spiritual forces in the world. A student back then would not just list Kether, Chokmah, Binah, and so on, they would combine them. For instance, to say “Kether Chesed Binah” was to proclaim a spiritual statement, that the highest spiritual power brings about intelligence through freedom, thereby designating higher beings who operate through this dynamic. This enough is true, that the task is to make these concepts roll around in the mind until they cease to be inert and become living realities.

With this in mind, it is then that we may return to Aristotle’s Categories properly. Aristotle’s Categrories are the Sephirot. They are not two different systems that share a superficial similarity, they are one and the same spiritual alphabet, just articulated in two different cultural idioms for two different peoples. In the times of Alexander the Great, when Greek and Jewish cultures met, both the Sephirot and the Aristotelian Categories were understood as the same thing, as a spiritual alphabet for reading the cosmos. The Jews had their ten spiritual letters, and the Greeks had their ten: Substance, Quantity, Quality, Relation, Place, Time, Position, Having, Action, and Affection. Both are in effect “trees of life”, listings of ten fundamental terms. The Categories of Aristotle are the West’s Sephirot, and the Sephirot are the East’s Categories. Both are the two great, complementary alphabets of their spiritual world, both expressing the same structural principles of reality.

The understanding that these systems are one was lost due to a historical process of forgetting (slow down, Heideggerians) that stripped these living concepts of spiritual content. The process began with the transition from Greek to Roman culture. The Greeks, when they spoke of Alpha, Beta, Gamma, etc., did not think of such abstract, meaningless letters. Alpha meant the spiritual man, Beta, the house in which spirit dwells, and so forth. Every letter was at the same time a name and an image, carrying a world of meaning unto itself. Over time, this process of graded abstraction delinked the power of words from their usage, resulting in the fall of language into a matter of convention. This fate befell both the Sephirot and the Categories. The Jewish disciples, named the Chachamim, were meant to carry on the tradition, but forgot the art of reading the Sephirot. They continued to list the ten names, but they no longer knew how to spontaneously conjure them in the applicable order to form spiritual sentences and statements. By the Middle Ages, they were arguing over the ‘correct’ combination of words like Hod, Chesed, Binah, treating them as fixed formulas rather than dynamic, combinatory letters. Similarly in the West, Aristotle’s Categories cemented themselves into the dry concepts of school logic textbooks. Being, property, relationship, etc. became nothing more than abstract common nouns. The Categories ceased being the structure of the world that the mind needed to submerge itself in to comprehend. Enough has been said on this tragic, but necessary, process, and much more can be said on Aristotle and the influence he has had on the world.

Pairings

Substance and Kether

For Aristotle, Substance is the primary category, because it is the being that underlies all other modes, that being the independent self-subsistence upon which everything else is predicated. Kether is the first Sephirah, the “crown” from which all remaining Sephirot unfold. It is the highest primary spiritual power from which all else derives. Both stand as the foundational principle upon which the entire structure rests. To call the primary reality “Substance” is to say that being is self-standing; Substance is the Greek mode of naming the primacy of the real, and Kether is the Jewish. Both are declaring that there is a first, ultimate ground that is not grounded in anything else. The ground of being is the very thisness of reality, and so is crowned as that which rules all.

Quantity and Chokmah

Quantity concerns extension, number, and magnitude, the measurable dimensions of a thing. Chokmah is wisdom, the first outflow from the Kether, the principle of all life, and the expansive wisdom that serves as an outpouring that multiplies and extends itself into creation. The correlation here is found in the principle of extension, quantity measures the outward extension of substance in the world, just as wisdom is the first outward movement of the divine in creation. To call the principle of extension Quantity, is to say that reality has a measure, and that it is a cosmos ordered by number and magnitude. To call it Wisdom is to say that this extension is intelligent, it is in many respects revealing of the Category and vice versa. The cosmos has number because it has wisdom; it has wisdom because it has number. The measure of things is the self-outpouring of divinity.

Quality and Binah

Quality determines what kind of a thing something is, that is to say, it’s essential character. Binah, as understanding, or intelligence, is the discerning that distinguishes one thing from another. Quality is what gives a thing its specific identity, Binah is the power that understands that specific identity by distinguishing it from what it is not. It’s worth nothing that the distinction is not as divorced as it is made out to be, particularly in man. It could be asked if a thing’s character exists independently of the thing’s understanding of it, but this is undercut by the fact that quality in man is itself in the fact of understanding. The knowability of the world is named Quality by the Greeks, and the elaboration that the Jewish concept brings is in the fact that this knowability knows itself by grasping itself. Ergo, the world has qualities precisely because it is knowable, and it’s knowability is in quality.

Relation and Chesed

Relation concerns itself with how one thing is with respect to another and to itself. Chesed is Mercy, Love, or Freedom as the expansive force which extends itself from itself to connect with the other. The very essence of relationality is in this movement, the self-gicing that establishes connections. To call the network of connections a relation is to say that reality is interconnected, and to call it Chesed is to say that this self-relation exists only by virtue of freedom, love, and mercy. It is a gift of self to itself. However this encounter may not always feel like a gift. No thing stands alone- to be is to be with, and the category of relation, or Chesed, is the rearticulation of a common substance that is held-together if not by love, then by some principle of cohesion.

Place and Geburah

Place is where a thing is. Geburah is severity, strength, and judgement. It is the force that sets limits and distinctions. Place is precisely about boundary; a thing is here and not there in place. Geburah is the principle of limitation and containment as a force that defines and restructs. The cosmos is structured because it is bounded, and so place, as the result of limit, is the strength that gives form by proclaiming “thus far and no further”. They are one and the same.

Time and Tiphereth

Time is the dimension of change and becoming. Tiphereth is Beauty. Beauty, in many classical senses, is harmony and proportion. Time, similarly, is the movement of things toward their fulfillment, to the degree that it tends towards a harmony of being. Tiphereth as the centrality of the higher and lower spiritual forces in the Kabbalistic tree is the heart of reconciliation. The cosmos in becoming becomes beautiful. Were Ahriman to have his way, he would prohibit this development, working from the past and freezing all into eternal repetition.

Position and Netsah

Position concerns the arrangement of parts and the stance of a thing. Netsah is victory, endurance, eternity, etc. The latter is the force of overcoming. Position is the result of the force that enables a thing to maintain its stance against that which would displace it, and so it can be said that every stance requires an overcoming of sorts. Surely, to have a position is to have won it, and to have a stance is to endure in such and such way. The Jews saw this category as a power, as the victory of holding one’s ground against the forces that would de-position it.

Having and Hod

Having can also be called condition in the sense that this category is taken to mean it has been conditioned. For this reason, it can also be called state. Hod is majesty, an outer radiance of glory that conceals the inner reality. Having is, then being concealed, or conditioned, by virtue of something which occludes the inner reality. Outward manifestation is the connection here. What a thing has is what it shows forth. The Greeks saw this as a condition; a thing has shoes, has arms, has a state of being. The Jewish formulation of this being an outreaching veil in the form of radiant glory is just another way of resasserting the presence of divinity in creation, despite how it hides an inner secret, requiring us to interrogate it for secrets. To be equipped is to be glorious. The king is equipped with his crown, the warrior his sword and armor, and the sage his wisdom manifest. Possession then really is a sort of manifestation.

Action and Yesod

To be equipped is to be able to act. Action is the active exercise of power upon something else. Yesod is the generative, grounding force that is the base upon which all action stands. All action is a kind of generation. At first, one might automatically pair Action with Netsah, seeing as Netsah sounds active, it is after all endurance. But if we follow the structure of the Kabbalisitc Tree, the higher determinations are gathered and transmitted downward toward manifestation. Action is similarly the category in which something passes outward into an effect. But it is only with Action that substance becomes agentic. It produces an effect beyond itself, and thus Yesod therefore corresponds to Action. All the prior Categories and Sephirot are gathered into an outgoing moment.

Affection and Malkuth

The final listing here, the Category of Being-Affected, or Affection, is the counterpart to the Action of Yesod. This completion takes place in the field, or kingdom, or Malkuth, the final Sephirah, where all the preceding forces manifest, the site where the spiritual becomes most material. Malkuth is the point of embodiment and realization, where that which comes from above is received into concrete actuality. All prior embodiment stands for Malkuth as its representative. It is in the kingdom, the realm of matter that relates to the physical world, that all Sephirot pour themselves out into, and as it’s correlate in Adam Kadmon shows through the feet, it is the most immediately accessible to earthly man. Likewise, it is less than easy for even the most uninquisitive minds to see the category of Being-Affected in the world.

The Four Causes and Four Worlds

Aristotle’s four causes present for us another avenue to explore when taken in consideration with it’s correlate. They are four different ways of explaining why something exists or happens. For Aristotle, a complete explanation often requires considering all four causes and not just the immediate physical cause. Listed forth they are as follows: the material cause which asks what something is made of (it’s matter), the formal cause which asks what its form is (its form), the efficient cause which asks what caused it, and the final cause which asks what it’s telos (final goal) is. We also have the four worlds of the Kabbalah, which describe four levels of reality, from the most spiritual to the more material. Firstly is the Atzilut, the world of Emanation. This is the highest level and the closest one to God, representing utterly divine presence. Next is Beriah, the world of creation. This is the realm of creation and intellect, where distinct spiritual beings and ideas begin to take form. Next is Yetzirah, the world of formation, where emotion and spiritual formation exists, associated with the shaping of spiritual forces, and finally there is Assiah, the world of action. This is the lowest level, representing the physical world and concrete action, the world we most readily experience.

Because the four worlds of Kabbalah describe the graded levels of being, a direct structural correlate can be found in the four causes wherein Atzilut corresponds to Final Cause, Beriah to Formal Cause, Yetzirah to Efficient Cause, and Assiah to Material Cause. In the same way that the four worlds are the categories of spiritual realms, the four causes act as a field by which one can relate the different registers of being provided by Aristotle’s Categories. Now, the four worlds are registers that interpenetrate all others, just as each cause operates as a dimension of explanation that interpenetrates all others. Meaning Aztiluth is not only the respective world of Final Cause, but the final cause register of every Sephirah and every Category, just as Beriah is the formal cause register of every Sephirah and Category, and so on and so forth. Substance then is not “in Assiah”, but instead is manifesting as Substance in all four registers, as the material substance, as the formative substance, as the formal/archetpal substance, and the emanative substance. The same holds for every Category.

Conclusion

Internalizing the Categories as one does the Sephirot, and truly comprehending them, is important insofar as it sanctions the capacity for genuine and valid cognition. Without it, thinking remains prone to a false subjectivity, grounded by nothing real. The modern mind has been trained to treat concepts any which way in relation to a world that is ultimately unknowable or indifferent. By not submerging oneself in these concepts, one remains trapped in what can only be called a prison of sorts, ignorant to the reality of things.

item.title: Epistle to Polygenism
item.description:
Intro

Human biodiversity confronts us with a problem. Among the myriad physical features of man such as skin color, muscle and fat distribution and composition, epicanthic folds, head and body shapes, hair, eye color, and even blood characteristics, it pushes one towards the verdict that we are in some way different. Yet, breeding within two “disparate” populations, producing fully fertile offspring is possible and we, more or less, are capable of communicating, interacting, and understanding the life of each other despite this unnamed difference. The problem we are confronted with is the imposition of difference, with the perceived ontological grounding of oneness. How can we be both one (a single species) and many (so visibly diverse)? An answer one often finds aligned with a paradoxically regressive strain of thinking is the conclusion of polygenism. Paradoxical since it seems to find a home among those who would ally with the bias of immediacy - such as those who call themselves Christians, or enlightenment thinkers that tend to biological reductionism. The answer they provide is accepting of the immediacy of appearance, as well as behavior, and reduces it to some immutable fact of biology, or in some cases denigrates the status of the spiritual by raising appearance and behavior to some discrete and exclusive spiritual condition. Either path is the aforementioned attitude in new skin, mentioned because of the elephant in the room: racism. More will be said on this later as it relates to racial distinctions. For now, only a footnote can be made on the racist, and often Faustian, motivations behind rejecting Out of Africa, as well as upholding the fixed character of “racial” distinctions.

One historical answer to the question of the one and many in man was polygenism, the view that different races have separate origins, whether created separately by God or evolved from different apes/hominids. The idea is quite old. For example, the Roman Emperor Julian argued that the Germani and Scythians were too different from the Ethiopians to share common ancestry. Oral traditions such as the Bambuti creation myth told of three races made from three different kinds of Clay. Biblical polygenism regularly draws on the three sons of Noah as stand in for the “races”, or stock, of Black, White, and Yellow. In the 19th century, polygenism became a scientific movement, drawing Enlightenment rationalism and empiricism into it’s supposed methodology. People like Samuel George Morton and Josiah Clark Nott claimed that cranial measurements proved races were separate species. Polygenism persisted, persisted even after Darwin’s Origin of Species, with Carl Vogt and others arguing that different races descended from different apes. These days, modern science has decisively rejected polygenism. The Out of Africa genetic evidence shows that all living humans trace to a common African population within the last 200-300 thousand years. There is no genetic or fossil support for separate origins. Polygenism seems to have failed because it mistook the superficial adaptations for a more prior difference.

As it appears, the rejection of polygenism does not dissolve the phenomenon of diversity. We are one species, one blood (especially after the time of Jesus), one recent origin. And yet we appear in such a variety. My own explorations of this topic takes the unity and diversity seriously as the starting point of a spiritual investigation. Polygenism as an Enlightenment project and mere stipulation was an enterprise dead on arrival, for mainly the same reasons that taxonomy fails at being a science. Taxonomy, which as much as it can list difference in painstaking detail, cannot arrive at the generative process by which the differences in the elements it categorizes come about. Likewise, it cannot supply us with what stands as a valid separation or not. Yet, it was not wrong to sense that the diversity we see has deep roots. What polygenism lacked was a vision of how unity could give rise to multiplicity without fracturing into separate species forever. This is where spiritual science may offer us a missing link in the fact that the diversity we observe is a result of a gradual hardening and differentiation from an original spiritual unity. The physical form we now call Homo sapiens is the ultimate consolidation of a long process that began when human souls first descended into Earthly bodies in the Lemurian epoch, passed through the more plastic, liquid forms of the Atlantean epoch, and only fully solidified in the Post-Atlantean - the very period that Out of Africa genetic studies takes as it’s given object.

Why has Out of Africa become the consensus view of modern anthropology? The reason is that the evidence for a recent African origin of Homo sapiens is now so extensive that alternative models, while interesting, have now been set as aside. This is the conclusion that I have ultimately come to. There are a few alternative theories to consider before returning to Out of Africa. The first is the Out of Australia theory. This hypothesis suggested that anatomically modern humans first emerged in Australia, based on the claims of very early archaeological sites like Lake Mungo, as well as the suggestion that some ancient Australian remains showed unique morphological features. Proponents of this theory argued that the long temporal depth of human occupation indicates a possible origin. The problem is that all living humans, including Indigenous Australians, carry the same genetic markers that trace back to Africa. The oldest Y-chromosome and mitochondrial DNA lineages are found in Africa, not Australia. Moreover, the oldest fossils of Homo sapiens are African, far predating any Australian remains. Early Australian sites indicate an early migration of modern humans out of Africa, as opposed to an independent origin. Hominin Network Theory, in recent years, proposes that the fact that Neanderthals and Denisovans interbred with modern humans, creating essentially a tangled web of interbreeding across Eurasia, suggests to us that modern humans did not have a single African origin, but rather emerged from a network of archaic populations across the Old World. This interpretation misreads evidence. Interbreeding did occur, although it was limited and one-sided. The Neanderthal and Denisovan DNA found in non-African populations amounts to only 1-6% of their genomes. The remainder is overwhelmingly derived from a single source population. Additionally, no trace of these archaic hominins exists in sub-Saharan African populations, who retain the oldest human lineages. The network model confirms that the African lineage was the dominant one, absorbing small contributions from archaic populations encountered during expansion. The multi-regional model proposed that after Homo erectus left Africa nearly 2 million years ago, populations in Africa, Europe, and Asia continued to evolve in parallel, with enough gene flow between them to keep them a single species. Modern humans, in this view, would have emerged simultaneously across the Old World from local archaic ancestors. For decades, this was the main competitor to Out of Africa. There was supporting evidence by some fossil evidence of regional anatomical continuity (such as the fact that certain facial features in East Asia seemed to persist from Homo erectus to modern populations). However, when ancient DNA became available, the multiregional model collapsed. Genetic data showed that all non-African populations carry a distinct genetic signature that emerged in Africa within the last 100,000 years and spread outward. There’s no continuity of lineages from pre-sapiens populations in Europe or Asia into modern humans. Only the small admixture noted prior. The scientific case for Out of Africa seems to be settled. But for those who ask why humans are so diverse, why this particular species expanded so rapidly, and what the meaning of our unity and diversity might be, science offers limited answers. The anthroposophic spiritual-scientific framework helps us to situate Out of Africa within a broader narrative, becoming material testament to spiritual reality.

Humans and Apes

Before continuing, it is important to note one thing. The animal kingdom (including the apes) did not arise through a linear evolution from lower to higher culminating in humans. Instead, animals represent forms separated from the human stream at various stages of Earth evolution. During the Lemurian and Atlantean Epochs, the human physical form remained relatively “plastic” and capable of being shaped by the will, while certain group souls took hold of physical bodies that had hardened prematurely, giving rise to the various animal species. Apes in particular are described as a branch that split off during the Lemurian epoch, when the human form was still soft. Their physical bodies became fixed earlier, while the human form retained its malleability, allowing it to later receive the fully incarnated human “I”. Thus, the anatomical similarities between apes and humans are not evidence of common descent in the Darwinian sense, it is a reflection of a shared origin in the plastic human form from which apes diverged. This has implications for how we interpret the fossil hominins such as australopithecines, Homo habilis, Homo erectus, and so on. They represent the various side branches or transitional forms that either preceded the full descent of the human “I” into physical bodies, or were left behind as the human form continued to refine and harden. The fact that the first stone tools appear with australopithecines shows that even before the “I” fully incarnated, beings with a degree of intelligence and will were interacting with the physical world. Steiner would likely say that these beings were ensouled by group souls (or by individual souls not yet fully independent) who were preparing the physical “vehicle” for the eventual incarnation of the fully self-conscious “I”. When we come to Homo sapiens in the Quaternary period, we see the completion of the process. The physical body is fully hardened, and the human “I” can incarnate into it with full self-consciousness/self-awareness. The Out of Africa populations can be said to represent the stock in which this final hardening and spiritual integration took place.

Physical Consolidation

The three periods we shall concern ourselves with are the Lemurian, Atlantean, and our current post-Atlantean epochs. The Middle Lemurian period, correlating roughly to the Mesozoic period, was the beginning of physical incarnation. The human body was still soft and malleable, bones were not fully mineralized, and so durable fossils did not exist. This was also following the time the sexed distinction made its emergence. The Atlantean period, correlating roughly to the Tertiary (the Paleogene and Neogene), found a progressive hardening of the world and of man. Bodies were much more liquid-like compared to today, yet the skeletal system was still not fully solid. The first durable artifacts of man appear only at the very end. It is with the Post-Atlantean period, correlating to the quaternary (Pleistoscene and Holocene), that “hardening” completed. Bones fully mineralized, the modern brain structure emerged (as evidenced by the Kalambo structure, demonstrating that even 500,000 years ago, beings on Earth were capable of planning and complex functions), and the human form as we know it today cemented itself. If Steiner’s account is accurate, we should expect the physical record to roughly correlate and show no durable evidence from the Lemurian epoch, because the body, and its lifestyle, did not leave much to be found. We should also find only sporadic, late evidence from the Atlantean epoch, as hardening gradually progressed (we will not touch the topic of inherited Atlantean wisdom in this article). Additionally, we should also find abundant evidence of fully modern humans from the post-Atlantean epoch onward. This is precisely what the fossil and archeological records reveal. During the Lemurian period, there are no accepted hominin fossils or stone tools. The few anomalous claims (such as the Eocene tools of the 19th century) have been refuted as either misinterpretations of the data or frauds. However, this does not serve as a problem, because it is exactly what one would expect if the human form has not yet reached a level of solidity capable of leaving durable remains (and based off the lifestyle of man during the Lemurian, they were much more nature attuned than we are today. The transformation/destruction of nature into tools would not occur until the Atlantean). For most of the period, there is no evidence of “man”. The first hominins appear only in the late Miocene and early Pliocene (Sahelanthropus, Orrorin, Ardipithecus), but they left no stone tools. Only at the very end of the Pliocene, around 3.3 million years ago, do we find the first undisputed stone tools at Lomekwi, Kenya. This is the point when Steiner would say hardening was approaching completion. As the Atlantean epoch gives way to the Quaternary, the first durable evidence of a being capable of thought and technology begins to appear. Finally, in the Quaternary period, with the beginning of the Pleistocene after the global flood, the picture begins to resemble what we are familiar with. We find the first fossils of Homo, the spread of stone tool industries across Africa and Eurasia, and eventually, around 300 thousand years ago, the appearance of the anatomically modern Homo sapiens. It is no coincidence that cognitive and technological sophistication became possible once the physical form had fully hardened. This, along with a myriad of other factors, such as the separation intwo sexes, made it possible for the kind of independent, discriminatory inner life we are familiar with today, including its offspring: technology.

The Out of Africa genetic evidence places the origin of all living Homo sapiens within the Post-Atlantean epoch. The mitochondrial and Y-chromosomal lineages that coalesce around 200-300 thousand years ago represent the survival of a particular population in Africa whose physical constitution had reached the modern level of mineralization. From this population all living humans have a connection. This does not mean that there were no humans before that time. It means that before the Post-Atlantean epoch, the human physical form had not yet achieved the degree of solidity that would allow it to fossilize in the kind of way we recognize today, and that the genetic lineages of those earlier forms either died out or were absorbed into the later, more hardened populations. In this way, the Out of Africa bottleneck is a genetic signature, representing the final stabilization of the modern human body.

Origin of the Races

If the human physical form only fully hardened in the Quaternary, then the diversity we see among human populations today must have arisen after that consolidation. For those that have followed thus far, this conclusion certainly makes sense. It is also consistent with the scientific view that the major physical differences among human groups are recent adaptations to different climates and environments, occurring within the last 100 thousand years or so. Steiner provides us with another, higher, aspect. The diversity we see appears to us as a matter of natural selection, or this or that theory, acting on a uniform “stock”. It may do something to that effect, but it primarily reflects the lingering influence of the spiritual forces that shaped the human body during the long epochs of hardening. The different “racial” characteristics are expressions of the different planetary and Luciferic influences that worked on the human form during the Lemurian and Atlantean epochs, only becoming fixed in the Post-Atlantean period.

In the middle of the Lemurian epoch, when the human physical form became capable of hosting the self-conscious “I”, souls began to incarnate from different planetary spheres (the beginning of physical existence, and the sexed distinction, was also the beginning of reincarnation!). This includes beings not only from Earth’s sphere, but also from Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, and other regions. These souls brought with them different spiritual-soul qualities, inclinations, temperaments, and karmic backgrounds that suited them for particular forms of earthly experience. The souls that descended from Saturn, for instance, had a natural affinity for a more inward, contemplative life; those that came from Mars brought a more active, will-oriented nature; those from Jupiter carried a certain wisdom and sense of the cosmic order. At that time, the human physical body was relatively malleable. The group souls that guided these incoming spirits worked from within to shape the body in accordance with the spiritual predisposition of each group. This is why, already in the Lemurian epoch, distinct “types” of humanity began to emerge. They would be tendencies that would later solidify into “races”.

An important factor in the formation of the races was the influence of the Luciferic beings. Luciferic spirits (particularly the aberrant Spirits of Form, also called the Luciferic Spirits of Motion) intervened in the evolution of humanity during the Lemurian and Atlantean epochs. Their goal was to accelerate the independence of the human “I” at the cost of disrupting the original unity of the human physical and etheric constitution. Had these beings not intervened, humanity would have developed from a single, uniform physical type that would have changed only slowly and in harmony with the Earth’s transformation. Instead, the Luciferic forces introduced differentiation. They hardened certain groups more quickly, fixed certain physical traits, and caused the stock of man to split into varied forms that adapted to different geographic and spiritual conditions. Steiner describes the abnormal Spirits of Form, working from the astral, taking hold of the etheric and physical bodies of different groups, imprinting them with characteristics that would later become hereditary. It’s important to clarify that these beings are not evil in the moral sense, but that their activity created the conditions for human diversity. While these also brought along with it the potential for egoism and separation, it also brought the need for the unifying force of the Christ impulse.

By the Atlantean epoch, the differentiation had crystallized into seven sub-races, from which the main racial types of the current Post-Atlantean epoch descended. At the end of Atlantis, when the continent was destroyed by the great flood (associated with the ice ages at the boundary between the Tertiary and Quaternary periods), populations migrated in different directions. According to Steiner, five main racial remnants emerged from this dispersal. I must mention importantly that these races are not to be confused with the modern day racial categories.

The first is the Black race, These are descendants of the earliest Atlantean sub-races, carrying the oldest physical forms. Their constitution is characterized by a strong astral body, making them receptive to spiritual forces in a more instinctive, dreamlike way. The next is the Yellow race, originating from the later Atlantean sub-races that migrated eastward into Asia. Their etheric body is particularly strong, giving them a higher rapport with the vital forces of nature, expressed in their languages and cultural forms. The next is the Red “American Indian” race, a branch that migrated westward into the Americas. They retained certain archaic qualities, including what Steiner calls a “memory-based consciousness”, and a close relation to the land. This red race of ancient times are not to be confused with the Native Americans of today, they represent a “declining” branch of humanity. More to be said on this later. The penultimate race is the Brown race, a mixed group which spread across the islands of Southeast Asia and the Pacific. Their physical form shows a blend of influences, and their constitution tends towards a certain dreaminess and passivity. Finally is the White race, descended from the fifth Atlantean sub-race (known as the “primal Semites”), which had its main center in what is now Ireland. This group migrated eastward across Europe and Asia, becoming the bearers of logical consciousness, the faculty that would come to full development in the Post-Atlantean epoch. Such migrations established the broad racial categories that have persisted into historical times. However, it is important to understand that the “races” we observe today are not identical to the original Atlantean forms. Over millennia, the intermixing with Homo sapiens and various other hominids, adaptation to new environments, and the ongoing process of soul incarnation have continuously reshaped these populations. The categories and characteristics that seem to hold so much weight today are in fact an outer residue of a process which began in the Lemurian period and is now gradually coming to the end.

As regarding the modern “races”, these five are definitely not “pure” types; they have intermingled throughout history well into our current Post-Atlantean period. The boundaries are fluid, and the characteristics attributed to the archaic races are general tendencies, not static absolutes. Migration and population is a very complex thing, involving moving over time, backflows of migration (creating a recursive situation), and internal differentiation within a given population. Throughout time, a tendency towards the flourishing of the individual has emerged, helped by the fact that Steiner emphasizes that these racial differences are not permanent. In the future, as humanity evolves toward spiritual unity, the concept of race will lose its meaning. For more on this, I have written The Problem of Africa in German Idealism and Anthroposophy’s Treatment as a Response to Afro-Pessimism

Each of the five main races is associated with a specific geographical region from which certain cosmic forces ebb and flow. Steiner indicates that there are five centers on Earth - in Africa, Asia, the Americas, and elsewhere - where the etheric forces that shape racial characteristics are concentrated. These centers are points through which planetary influences (the same planets that hosted the descending souls) work on the human constitution. The Lemurian and Atlantean epochs were the periods of race formation, a time when the physical and etheric bodies of man were molded into distinct types under the influence of spiritual beings. The Post-Atlantean epoch, by contrast, is the period of soul development. The task for this epoch is not to create new races (although one trip to New York and you will find combinations never before conceived, Yemeni-Puerto Ricans and Bengali-Russians alike). It is a time for the cultivation of the individual “I”, enabling man to overcome the limitations of heredity and race. This is why, in the Post-Atlantean epoch, the concept of race loses its significance. The five main races, therefore, are remnants of an earlier stage of evolution. Their continued existence serves a purpose only insofar as they provide a variety of physical and etheric conditions through which the soul can gain a kind of training, but the direction of evolution is towards unity. Like a teacher who has finished teaching a student erases their vocation, leaving behind a learned pupil, so too shall the racial conditions serve their purpose for the development of man.

Adam and Eve Revisited: One and Too Many

What is left after the initially unified “man” having been a purely spiritual form, then concretized and materialized into the many kinds of man, is revealed to be a transitionary stage towards a reunion of unity? We may bring to the fore the archetypes which underlie the unity of man: Adam and Eve. It is quite fitting that modern science has taken the symbolic archetypes found in the bible in its monikers of “Y-chromosomal Adam” and “Mitochondrial Eve”. The familiar biblical account of Adam and Eve has long been read as the story of two individual human beings, the first man and woman from whom all humanity descended. Modern genetics has shown that this literal interpretation cannot stand. There was no “first man” or “first woman” in the sense of a solitary breeding pair. Yet the truth of the narrative, properly understood illuminates the findings of the mineralistic sciences. We will re-appropriate these figures in order to help us understand them as the primal polarity of group spirit and group soul, and check the unending modulation of the one and many.

The two figures are not physical individuals. They represent the group spirit/soul of nascent humanity. Adam (“the one taken from the earth”) stands for the unified “I-being” of humanity, or in other words, the collective spiritual identity from which all individual human spirits descend. Eve (“the animate one”, or “the mother of all living”) represents the group soul, the diversifying principle that gives form to the physical, etheric, and astral bodies of human beings across the Earth. Spiritually, we are one. All human souls share the same origin in the Adam-I. Physically, we are many. The Eve-soul differentiates itself into the varied forms and temperaments that allow souls to undergo the experience and training necessary for their evolution.

The more esoteric connection between the names Yahweh and Eve goes even further. Yahweh, the “Earth Lord”, is the being who guides the development of the human “I” on Earth. The name Yahweh contains the Yodh, which represents the individual I-being, that glimmer of selfhood that descends into the human soul. Eve, as the “Earth Mother” embodies the accumulated forces of the Old Saturn, Old Sun, and Old Moon stages of Earth evolution, forces which build the physical, etheric, and astral bodies that serve as a dwelling place for the “I”. Thus in the name “Yahweh”, we have the union of the spiritual I (the Adam principle), with it’s concretized form (the Eve principle). This union is the true “first couple”, the foundational polarity of spirit and soul that makes human existence on Earth possible. With this in mind, the apparent contradiction between man’s genetic unity and physical diversity dissolves. The one is the Adam-I, the unified spiritual origin of all human beings. Every human soul, regardless of race or epoch, participates in the same I-being. This is partly why, despite all the outward differences, we can recognize one another as fellow humans, why the deepest spiritual development always leads to the experience of a universal brotherhood. The differences end up negligible. The “many” is the Eve-soul, the variable manifest as the variety of physical forms, temperaments, and cultural expressions. The Eve-soul is a collective soul that “gives birth” to the multiplicity of human forms. Hence, from a single spiritual stock, diversity in man can come about.

Through the development of the “I”, and reception of the Christ impulse, individuals can increasingly free themselves from the constraints of heredity and race. The Pauline saying, that “There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus” makes this goal express. The reunification of the many into one, without the loss of individuality, is a foregone conclusion.

item.title: Ontic Limitations and the Disappearance of the Event: Developmental Recursions Re; Modern Spirituality and Philosophy
item.description:
Ontic Limitations

Modern cognition crowns reason and logos as it’s chief modus operandi. Conjure in mind the current world of cognition, of logical relations and the system resulting from this network. A world is rightfully identified as a system of relations, and so the current world of cognition we inhabit will be roughly identified as the world of logos; the world of relationality and self-reflexive deliberation. However, given the nuggets of wisdom provided such figures as Alfred North Whitehead, Jean Gebser, Heraclitus, Hegel, Nagarjuna, and Aztec metaphysics, in other words, the form of procedural generation, that of an inscribing of the self movement of being, it would be unwise to consider this modernity as static and eternal. Logos did not appear spontaneously. Emerging from a prior condition, just as adult emerges from child, or plant from seed, every developed faculty rests on a simpler faculty which makes the genesis of a new faculty possible in the first place. If we take our current cognition for granted, we overlook the fact that it had to be built up in some way or form. Thus, we may be permitted to conceive of a differing cognition that inches ever so slowly towards the kind we are familiar with. This priority is given to the faculty of memory. Before man could think abstractly, he needed to be able to hold the past steadily before him. Any application of a universal rule a la the logic principle must recognize a present situation which resembles a past one, that is to say, a line of self-continuity would need to be established, and prior to that, the establishment of continuity at the most basic level. This act of base level continuity in question is the faculty of memory. The capacity for stable, pictorial recollection acts as the previous interiority of an earlier phase of human development, present in weakened form even now in certain animals. It was out of this ground that logos would sprout from. Consider what logos demands. To operate, one must hold multiple elements in mind simultaneously, and to compare, one must retain one image (or concept for the modern bias, we will address this shortly) while inspecting and appraising another. To reason, you must remember that A preceded B, and so without a reliable faculty of memory, none of these operations are possible. The abstract thinking prized of modern man is in fact impossible without a stable foundation of concrete recollection. If memory is a prerequisite for logos, then memory had to have been developed before logos could arise. And if it was developed, then there was a development when memory was the most novel, the most advanced, or highly developed faculty that human cognition possessed. It was the cutting edge of humanity, because it was humanity’s function, just as we rightfully say that the current activity of man, thinking, is what characterizes him today. This period and system of relations is what can be called the world of memory. It is the cognitive epoch in which the retention of percepts was the supreme human achievement, prior to the emergence of logic. In that world, memory was not the tool serving thought, because there was no “thought” as we know it. Memory during this period was thought, as the highest faculty defining the entire horizon of what the human mind could do and be. What is asked is not to abandon logos in this ensuing conception, but to recognize that our current mode of cognition has a history, and that exploring this mode of cognition thoroughly will yield insights about our current.

The World of Memory

Now let us attempt to reconsitute this world of memory and draw out the implications. Consciousness would not present itself as it does today with a mental space, or mind’s eye, where one holds abstract disembodied concepts like “justice”, “number”, “freedom”, “causality”, and so forth. Rather, the mind is a continuous streaming gallery of sensory impressions. Every situation encountered is re-cognized rather than anaylzed. When looking at a particular arrangement of stones, one would not in their mind’s eye see things like weight or measure, one would instead have a picture of a similar arrangement of stones arise in mind, perhaps witnessed in youth, when your father placed them that way for a purpose. This remembrance carries the full sensory intensity of the original; the warmth of the sun, the texture of the stone, and so on in this memory constitute understanding. Nothing is added into it,one lets the stones speak for themselves. Reasoning, similarly, is reconstituted. What we call reasoning now would be transformed, or rather reverted, into the natural resonance of one vivid picture calling forth others. The reasoning we have now links concepts together through logical connectivity, but the reasoning in the world of memory links memories together with a kind of negativity brought by the selfsame movement of experience. When one faces a decision, there is no weighing of pros and cons. You simply let the present scene invoke a cascade of similar past scenes, and the most compelling picture, that is the one that feels most familiar and densely textured, governs your action. Time is gone; all that exists is an eternal now that is thick with the accumulated weight of everything you have ever experienced. Past is known, surely, but future is the mere difference of now, nothing but a new situation that in turn becomes part of this eternal now. What of the social substratum? What of the social order and organization? Because memory is the supreme faculty, authority rests solely with the old. The person who has lived many decades has a storehouse of pictures and sensory impressions so vast and so finely differentiated that no young person could ever hope to match it. Any situation that presents a threat to the social whole finds the youngest silent and the elders conferring. Keep in mind they do not debate, since this would call into question the status of things like the reason embodied in an individual, they instead confer by calling forth the pictures of every previous similar threat and every succesful remedy. The elder who can summon the most relevant and most powerful picture leads. Even education is subject to this crowning activity of man- when one is a child, they were not taught rules or laws or given multiplication tables or grammatical structure. Instead, a child would be shown life in its fullness by the teacher, an older relative or respective elder with the authority to pass on memories, performed the acts of planting, building, healing, etc. in front of you. They would not explain the principles, firstly because they couldn’t, and secondly because letting you see the act in it’s complete context, with all its attendant sounds, emotions, colors, warmths, and so on, would prove much more effective in internalizing it. Years later, when faced with a similar task, that entire lived scene returns to oneself intact. In a way, it is like downloading a scene, and re-enacting it. Finally, the structure of communal ownership we have now would make no sense in a world of memory. The concept of “ownership” does not make sense. Everyone is always-already embedded in a web of shared experiences, and so the grove of trees that provided shelter for your people is simply there, as a fixed point in the collective memory.

To be aware of this world of memory as the pre-requisite to a sort of frontier beyond would not make much sense, at least, in terms of this world as beings in the world of memory, it is a full world. It is a complete and self-sufficiently integrated form of human existence. It is only from our current mode of consciousness, that of the self-reflective and abstract thinking kind, that we may even reconstitute it in the first place. To speak of the world of memory, it is prengant with the fruits of our current cognition today; structureud by subjects and objects, sequence, causality, and by the very logical relations that the world of memory supposedly lacks. This means that every description of the world of memory is a translation from a language we do not speak into a language we do. The very instant we say that “in that world, cognition is not a re-presentation, or an abstract hypostasis of self-generating conceptuality”, we are generating it in mind without living it. We are subjecting a non-logical state, or perhaps an unconsciously logical state, to logical form. We cannot avoid this. Because we are logical beings, our positive descriptions of the world of memory are necessarily metaphorical. However, our negative descriptions are precise, and so we can say it is not sequential, that in our world cognition moves from premise to conclusion, from thinking to the world. In the world of memory, these distinctions are absent, we can only say that this structure is absent and indicate towards a rudimentary structure currently present, but highly developed. We can say that it is not abstract, that our thinking metamorphoses through particularity to arrive at universality, that the world of memory acts only particular as a reified pseudo-universal. We may even say that it is not detached, that there is no gap between knower and known, because the concept of knower and the concept of known does not exist, only the immediate unity of knowledge- yet even this is a metaphor drawn from our experience of separation. The deeper implication of this exercise is that when we describe the world of memory, we are in effect describing our own current cognition by proxy, since by the very act of description, including it’s structure and limitations, it reveals what we are by the activity we undertake. Consider this: when we say that the world of memory does not calculate, this statement itself is a kind of calculation as a judgement of comparison, or in other words, a logical operation. So our description of a non-logical state is itself logical. The content says “no logic”, but the form is logic. There is a recursive knot presenting itself. We cannot step outside our own cognition to describe a radically different cognition, because the very articulation of it is an act of our cognition. Any world, or system of relations, that we posit is, in its very formulation, an object of our current knowing. It cannot estape being filtered, shaped, and constituted by the very faculty we are attempting to examine. The most that can be afforded to knowledge of the world of memory is that we may gain a glimpse of what it is like since implicitly we have already gone through that development, seeing as logic is grounded by what may be called here memory.

However, this can’t be said for any future cognition. Take these conclusions and apply them to our current mode of cognition and the frontier beyond our current mode. Just as the leap from memory to logic was a structural transformation, so too will there be a leap from logic to something beyond. However, if we take this principle seriously, we must admit that we can say the frontier is not logic, just as logic was not memory, and that the frontier will sublate logic, just as logic sublated memory, and that the frontier will reveal the limitations of logic, just as logic revealed the limitations of memory. But we cannot say what the frontier is using logical conception. Any attempt to do so would be a logical proposition of a post-logical state, which itself is invalid by the standards of the world of logos. It would be like a memory-based being trying to describe a logical syllogism using only remembered pictures, only pointing to the absence of pictures, but never generating the syllogism itself. The frontier then can be described as a structural inevitability, as a determined corollary of the fact that our current cognition is one stage in a process. Its only accessible quality is its otherness relative to us, and thus, only a negative standpoint can be had with respect to it.

Concrete Reality a la Atlantis

Assuming that the development of consciousness makes itself real at the same time as it’s conceptual development, we should expect to see this world of memory in the world and not let it collect dust as a logical inference or abstract philosophical construct. It should be discoverable as an actual phase of human experience, with its own characteristic forms of life and cognition. This is precisely what Rudolf Steiner, among others, describes. In his account of human evolution, this “world of memory” existed as a historical reality in a period he called the Atlantean epoch, during which memory was the most novel, and most developed faculty of human consciousness. Before logic and abstract reasoning, before that rule-bound thinking we now use colloquially, there existed a phase in which pictorial retention was the very substance of thought. Steiner’s descriptions match up exactly with what a logically reconstituted world of memory could provide. Man remembered, and called forth living pictures of the past. The words of Atlantean man carried force instead of meaning. Man’s techne, still being embedded in nature, was drawn from the formative forces they could still perceive. Additionally, physical nature and the environment is radically unlike our own during these times. Man’s physical constitution is described as watery, consisting of soft cartilage rather than hard bone, and covered by a thin, net-like skin. The head, in particular, was hydrocephalic in form, resembling the head of a human embryo, with a very high forehead. Speaking of the head, this idea that the brain excretes ideas like the liver excretes bile is relatively modern. Steiner reports that during these times, thinking was not a function of the solid brain. Instead, the Altantean could think with the water of his own bodily fluids. When this water element receded and the body hardened, the capacity for that form of thinking was lost, and the low-skulled forms (like the Neanderthal) appeared as a transitional phase before the modern high forehead grew back. Earthly conditions supported this constitution, as they always do (in the sense that there is a commensurability between an organism and it’s environment). The air enveloping the Earth was much denser than it is now, and the water over the entire earth was significantly more “fluid”, which was a crucial condition for the technology of the time. The geography of the Earth was entirely different as well. This should give an idea for the time frame of the Atlantean epoch. All of this corresponds precisely to what we would expect from a period in which memory was the cognitive frontier.

The faculty of memory itself can be given a broad summation, however, Steiner actually details the novelties that different collectives of peoples during the Atlantean epoch develop. Meaning, surely, the faculty of what we call memory now is the activity of human being, but the history of the races he describes are the sequential stages of that activity’s development through time. Beginning with what he identifies as the Rmoahal race, what they mark is the magic of speech, of words that directly affect nature, then the Tlavatli, who bring about ambition and ancestor-worship, wher memory serves personal recognition. The individual shows signs of emergence, beginning to feel their own value, seeing as leaders are elected based on something individual. Then the Toltecs, who bring about commonwealths and hereditary dynasties- statecrafts built on shared memory. These are the first stable, harmonious societies. Education here transfmits ability from father to son. Next are the Primal Turanians, who innovate the use of black magic, or rather the misuse of the life-force sanctioned by the Rmoahals for selfish desires. Because the principle of individuation already began to show it’s hand, so too has the origin of egoism been birthed and the betrayal of spiritual secrets. The Primal semites followed, marking the beginning of logical thought and interiorization as the birth of abstraction and the loss of mastery over life-force. Penultimately are the Akkadians who mark the emergence of law and legislation, where external order replaces shared memory. The novelty in the world here is of restlessness, of enterprise, colonization, and commerce. Finally, the last race marking the overarching development of Atlantean consciousness are the Mongolians. The race group here represents a mystical conservatism that holds onto the ancient past while losing its living power. This (sub)race develops thought-power, but retains a nostalgic residue of the older memory faculty and the qualities of the fourth sub-race. Note: the modern populations using these terms do not correspond to the racial terms used. Now, the entire sequence is the slow and painstaking birth of the individual thinking ego, out of the oceanic picture-consciousness of nature. Whenever a new faculty develops, an old one must wane. The very power of memory, which allowed mastery over life, was destined to fade as the faculty of logical thinking began to emerge, and so memory, being tied to the past and to nature, lack the capacity to restrain selfishness. It could vividly recall personal power and achievements, which fed ambition. This is precisely why the higher faculty of thought had to emerge: to check the destructive misuse of life-force. By the time the fifth sub-race appears, logical thought has begun to eclipse memory, and with that loss comes the loss of command over the external forces of nature. The price of inner freedom, that is to say the ability to say “I”, is the loss of outer, magical participation in the world.

Even now, we may look to the world of logos and track it’s development. The thinking of the Greeks, for instance, is nothing like the abstract thinking of the current year. During the times of Plato and Socrates, thinking rightly was inseparable from living rightly. Genuine knowledge of the Good was meant to transform the thinker into a better person. Modern rationality, by contrast, can be extraordinarily intelligent and logical while remaining morally neutral, and so a person can be both highly rational and deeply immoral. The reason for this is the evolution of consciousness currently happening, where thinking, this process of internal life generation, needs to exhaust it’s own functions fully and become more and more abstract, detached from the external world until it can arrive at goodness independently in the ego. Because the ego must learn to generate goodness from within itself and not inherit it from cosmic order or externality, it must withdrawal itself from the world, allowing the reality of the intelligently bad person.

Now, this brings us back to the relative relativity of cognition. If every cognitive faculty is bound by its developmental stage, then how can we trust any description of a future or prior epoch? Steiner himself presents a very curious case we will return to later, related to this relativity. For now, it should be noted that for Steiner, the manner in which he describes Atlantis is more of a documented phase. It is, for him, not using the modern, abstract rationality we are familiar with. He claims to be providing a positive account for the future cognition in which reason is the lowest form of the kind of activity man is made to do (what he calls clairvoyance). The faculties he employs are latent in us but currently underdeveloped, and so his descriptions are perceptions made possible by a cognitive apparatus that has already begun to evolve in us, beyond the purely logical. Yet, when he speaks to us, he must translate those perceptions into our language. He must use concepts, sequences, categories, and metaphors that our current minds can grasp. Meaning, even Steiner’s descriptions to us are subject to the cognitive horizon. They are approximations, shaped by what we are capable of receiving. The good news is that this itself is very economical of being. In effect, it is being offering it’s own humility and inadequacy. Human being articulates its own finitude with respect to what is beyond it and subjects itself to the understanding of what is there. Surely, if reality were fully transparent to us at our current stage, no development would occur. We would have arrived and there would be no growth or freedom. The fact that we cannot fully describe the world of memory or the spiritual world is being’s way of witholding itself so that we might become worthy of it. That the current mode of cognition overdetermines all things and claims absolute knowledge is only testament to the fact that it is a form of evil; of finite being self-perpetuating itself without limit.

The Disappearance of the Event

Heidegger’s Archimedean Point and Steiner’s Path

The ontic limit is the horizon of ordinary human cognition. Human being, in the current waking consciousness, is structurally attuned to entities in the form of their concepts, perceviging what is present, what acts, what causes, and what is caused. It organizes these perceptions (perceptions here does not only mean empirical items, it may include concepts themeselves) through logical categories, causal frameworks, propositional forms, and abstract logics as a required stage for the emergence of the independent ego and for the practical mastery of the sensory world by the very same. However, this itself represents a limitation of sorts. The fundamental question is whether human cognition can articulate realities that exceed its current state. The ordinary condition of consciousness, ordinary meaning current, is bound to the aforementioned organization above. And so to speak even of a grasping of consciousness itself, let alone the living Christ and Trinity, requires a movement beyond the conceptual inventory defining modern rationality and logos. Now, such a movement can’t possibly be an abandonment of logic unless one is committed to the idea that thought does not change, that thought has been like this since the beginning of humankind, throughout eternity. Such a position will not be entertained here. The human being is not trapped within its current cognitive horizon, in fact, they themselves can become conscious of their own limitations, and this self-consciousness is itself the first step toward surpassing the limitation.

Note: It is through the wheel of dharma and through the successive process of reincarnation (as well as initiation for the chosen few) that this self-realization takes place.

Heidegger can demonstrate for us that the modern understanding of truth is actually quite derivative. Truth, in the contemporary world, is understood as the correctness of a proposition in relation to a fact, of thought to being, or of concept to object. This can be called a generalized correspondence theory, that some idea assert itself and find itself in the world as a state of affairs. And so Heidegger locates the origin of this current ontic limitation in the transformation of the experience of truth. For the pre-Socratics, truth was known as aletheia, or unconcealment. It was the event of beings emerging into the open. Truth primarily was not a property of propositions or concepts and the world disclosed itself to the human being, and the human being dwelt within this disclosure. Subject and object were not yet rigidly separated. Plato initiated the split. By positioning the Forms as the truly real and the sensible world as a realm of appearance, Plato reoriented philosophy toward the correct apprehension of an intelligible realm, and the metaphor of vision became central. The philosophy turns his gaze toward the Forms and sees correctly. Truth then become the correctness of beholding. This transformation certainly was not an error. As explained prior, this was a step required for the emergence of the independent ego, but the risk that this change brings is in Truth ceasing to be the event of disclosure. Truth is now the correspondence of representation (or concept) to object. The subject stands now over against the object, measuring its assertions against the object’s perceived properties. This is the theory of truth that dominates modernity. Heidegger then claims that before we can assert that a proposition corresponds to some thing, the tree must have already disclosed itself as something that can be encountered.
